newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS-NZ brewer DB says swimming against beer tide.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-NZ brewer DB says swimming against beer tide.

text.p: New Zealand brewer and drinks firm DB Group Ltd said on Wednesday it faced continued pressure on its core beer market and would struggle to match first half earnings growth in the second part of the year.

Commenting on results that showed first half net profit rising slightly more than market expectations to NZ$17.2 million ($11.9 million) from $16 million a year ago, DB said it hoped a decline in beer sales would ease later in the year.

Despite the strong performance the group's Dutch chief executive Erik Korthals Altes warned he was not very confident DB would be able to sustain the eight percent-plus profit growth rate achieved in the six months to the end of March.
DB is majority owned through a Heineken NV and Fraser and Neave Ltd joint venture.

Asked if he expected a better second half, Korthals Altes said: "That would be nice, but we know what we did in the first half and I'm not overly confident that we will be able to maintain that eight-plus (growth) in the rest of the year."
In the reported period sales revenue fell slightly to $351 million but the company raised its operating profit by eight percent to $24.6 million.
Korthals Altes said the New Zealand beer market declined 5.4 percent in the year to March, which was equivalent to more than 20 million litres with a "staggering" retail value of $80 to $100 million.
After what he called a terrible 1995/96 winter in volume terms, DB expected to pick up a little during the impending winter season, he told a news conference.

However, with the latest sales data showing volumes in April down 10 percent on the year-ago period and a six percent drop in May, DB was still struggling against the tide and he predicted an overall consumption decline of four or five percent for the year as a whole.
DB said that alongside the consumption slippage, the New Zealand market would continue to be highly competitive for all products in its beer, wine and spirit brand portfolios.
While spirits and liqueur volumes were now starting to fall, this was being offset by what the company called huge growth in its ready-to-drink range.

"The directors have every confidence that the group will produce a satisfactory result for the full year based on the consistent implementation of brand-building policies in all its core markets," it added in its results statement.
However, executives gave no further insight into what might be considered satisfactory in the current market climate.
In its comment on sales of Heineken beer in the local market, DB said first half sales had outstripped the most optimistic forecast, but again gave no further details.

The firm restructured its balance sheet in May, resulting in the cancellation of three out of four fully-paid shares, and analysts have said one of the implications of the rejig will be to make the company a net payer of interest in the second half.
Analysts expect full-year profit of around $24 million, partly reflecting this changing in financing costs.
DB shares moved up three cents to NZ$2.25 on the stock market after the results, amid positive sentiment over the company's ability to maintain profits against the market trend.
"Operationally it was a good result, particularly in a market that has been declining, in terms of the overall beer market," broker Vicki St John said at First NZ Capital said.
By contrast, DB's main competitor, the larger Lion Nathan, in April reported a 21 percent slump in its first half profit to NZ$72.2 million.
Lion blamed competitive markets in both New Zealand and Australia for the decline, plus a slightly higher tax rate. (US$=1.44NZ$)
